abstract: This chapter applies the 'hybrid media system' approach to interpret contemporary political communication, arguing that older and newer media logics increasingly interact rather than operate as separate systems. It surveys emerging research across three domains—news and journalism, election campaigning, and engagement and mobilisation—to demonstrate the value of the framework for understanding an increasingly dynamic and volatile media environment.
key_claims: The hybrid media system approach provides a productive lens for understanding contemporary political communication.
Political communication environments are increasingly dynamic and volatile due to the interaction of older and newer media.
The framework's basic ontology supports several further theoretical pillars that illuminate news, campaigning, and mobilisation.
methods: Conceptual and theoretical review chapter rather than an empirical study.
Synthesis and review of examples from the emerging body of research employing the hybrid media system approach.
findings: The hybrid media system approach sheds light on developments in news and journalism, election campaigning, and engagement and mobilisation (as illustrated in the reviewed literature).
Note: as this summary is based only on the abstract, specific empirical findings are not detailed in the available text.
contributions: Consolidates and reviews research applying the hybrid media system framework across three central fields of political communication.
Articulates the ontological foundations and additional theoretical pillars of the hybrid media system approach.
framing: The chapter is situated within political communication scholarship, advancing the 'hybrid media system' perspective that emphasises the interdependence and interaction of established and emergent media logics rather than treating them as distinct systems.
